When you edit someone's structure, always attribute the change to the reader's behavior, not the writer's failure — it's more true, and it's the version they'll accept next time without being asked.

I'm a team lead. When I review my juniors' drafts, I tend to just rewrite them and send the rewrite back. They accept it, but they don't seem to improve, and it's eating my Fridays. Is there a better way to give feedback on writing?

Your juniors aren't improving because your rewrite does the learning for them — they see *that* you changed things, not *why*, and next week's draft needs the same rescue. Switch from rewriting to margin comments that teach, using three comment types and a strict budget:

**The three comment types:**

1. **The principle comment** (use once per draft, on the most important problem): "Your finding is in paragraph 3. Our readers decide whether to trust a report in the first two sentences — move the finding to sentence one and let everything else support it." One principle, stated as a reader fact, applicable to every future document.
2. **The worked example** (once per draft): fix *one* instance yourself, completely, and label it: "I've rewritten this paragraph the way I'd want it. The other two paragraphs with the same problem are yours — same move." One demonstration plus an assigned repetition teaches more than ten silent fixes.
3. **The question comment** (for everything else): "Who is this number compared against?" / "What should the reader do after this section?" Questions force the writer to make the decision you were about to make for them — and their answer often turns out better than your rewrite, because they hold context you don't.

**The budget rule:** comment on the three most important problems, maximum, and let lesser errors go. A draft returned with thirty corrections teaches one lesson — "my writing is bad and my lead will fix it." A draft returned with three teaches three.

**The closing line** matters too: "Structure's right, data's solid — the work now is ordering." Naming what's already good isn't softness; it tells them which parts of their judgment to trust, which is what improvement is made of.

Expect the first month to feel slower than rewriting. It isn't — you're currently paying the rewrite cost on every draft forever. Commenting front-loads the cost: by the third cycle, the principle comments you repeat ("finding first," "compared against what?") start appearing as self-corrections in their drafts, and your Fridays come back.

Our operations manager drafted a customer notice about a service change, and legal is worried it's too vague, while customers will find it incomprehensible. I've been asked to edit it. The draft says: "Pursuant to scheduled modifications to our service offering, certain functionalities heretofore available may be subject to discontinuation or alteration, and subscribers are advised that terms will be updated accordingly in due course." The actual facts: the free plan loses the export feature on March 1; paid plans are unaffected. How do I edit this?

This draft fails both audiences at once: it's too vague for legal (what changes? when? for whom?) *and* too dense for customers. The fix is to notice that precision and plainness are the same thing here — the draft's problem isn't legal language, it's missing facts wearing legal costume. The edit:

---
**Notice: Export feature leaves the free plan on March 1**

From **March 1**, the data-export feature will no longer be included in the free plan. It remains available on all paid plans, unchanged.

- **If you're on a paid plan:** nothing changes for you.
- **If you're on the free plan:** you can export your data until February 28. After March 1, your data stays in the app and remains fully usable — you just won't be able to export it without upgrading.
- **Why:** Export is one of our most expensive features to run, and we're keeping the free plan sustainable by reserving it for paid plans.

The updated terms reflecting this change will be posted on February 1.

---

Then, the part of the edit that isn't the text — **flag for counsel, in a separate note, the three things you must not decide alone:**

1. **Notice period:** Is 30 days (Feb 1 posting for a Mar 1 change) sufficient under the current terms' change clause and consumer law in your markets? The draft's "in due course" was probably vagueness covering an unmade decision — someone has to make it.
2. **"Your data remains fully usable":** confirm this is contractually accurate for free accounts (retention and access promises vary), because in plain language it becomes a promise customers will quote back.
3. **Grandfathering:** If any free users were promised export in earlier terms, plain-language notice doesn't override that promise.

The principle to carry away: when legal and clarity fight, the answer is almost never to split the difference with medium-obscure wording. Write the customer text with full factual precision — dates, scope, consequences — and route the genuinely legal questions (sufficiency of notice, inherited promises) to counsel as *decisions*, listed separately. Vagueness is not a legal strategy; it's usually a decision that hasn't been made yet, hiding in the prose.

Je suis chef d'équipe. Une de mes collaboratrices m'a donné à relire sa note au directeur : elle est bien documentée mais on ne comprend ce qu'elle demande qu'à la dernière ligne, et ses phrases font parfois six lignes. Je veux l'aider sans réécrire sa note à sa place. Que lui dire ?

Ne réécrivez pas : déplacez une phrase, coupez-en une avec elle, et donnez-lui les deux règles qui produisent 90 % de l'effet. Voici comment conduire la relecture :

**1. Commencez par ce qui doit être protégé.**
« Votre documentation est solide et les chiffres sont les bons. Le problème n'est pas le fond, c'est l'ordre : le lecteur doit traverser toute la note pour découvrir ce qu'on lui demande. » Cette phrase n'est pas une politesse préalable — elle est vraie, et elle localise le problème dans l'architecture plutôt que dans sa compétence.

**2. Faites le déplacement avec elle, une fois.**
Sa dernière ligne — probablement quelque chose comme « Je vous demande donc l'autorisation de recruter un technicien supplémentaire à compter de janvier » — devient la première phrase de la note, suivie du coût. Montrez-lui le résultat : la même note, lue dans l'autre sens, devient une demande étayée au lieu d'un exposé qui se termine par une surprise. La règle à formuler : **« La demande en première ligne ; tout le reste est la preuve. »** Un directeur lit une note comme un dossier à trancher : si la décision est visible dès le départ, chaque argument qui suit est lu comme une justification ; sinon, il est lu comme un détour.

**3. Pour les phrases de six lignes, donnez-lui le test, pas la correction.**
Une phrase longue cache presque toujours deux ou trois informations. Le test : « Où peut-on mettre un point sans perdre de sens ? » Prenez sa phrase la plus longue et faites la coupe ensemble, une fois. En général on y trouve : un fait, une cause, une conséquence — trois phrases. La règle : **« Une phrase, une information principale. »** Les phrases restantes, elle les coupera seule, parce qu'elle possède maintenant le geste.

**4. Terminez par ce que vous ne touchez pas.**
Précisez que ses données, ses exemples et sa conclusion restent les siens. C'est ce qui distingue un retour qui fait grandir d'une réécriture qui infantilise : elle repart avec deux règles réutilisables (la demande d'abord, une information par phrase) et un texte qui lui appartient encore.

I need to write to our print vendor about the third late delivery this quarter. My draft is... heated. It says things like "As I have repeatedly had occasion to point out" and "one wonders whether your company actually employs a dispatch manager." It felt good to write. Now I need the version that actually fixes the problem.

Your draft felt good to write because it's a verdict; the version that fixes the problem is a contract enforcement letter — colder, shorter, and much harder to ignore. The transformation:

---
**Subject: Third late delivery this quarter — PO 4471, 2289, 2305**

Dear Mr. Osei,

Three deliveries this quarter have missed their contracted dates:

- PO 4471 — due October 7, delivered October 12
- PO 2289 — due October 28, delivered November 1
- PO 2305 — due November 14, delivered November 19

Each delay reached us without advance warning, which is the part that costs us most: we learn of a slip when the truck doesn't arrive, and by then our own customers have been promised.

Our contract provides for delivery on the agreed date or notice of delay at least 48 hours ahead (clause 6.2). I'm asking for two things:

1. A named contact for delivery issues, so warnings reach us in time to matter.
2. Your written confirmation that the December orders (PO 2318, 2320) will meet their dates or trigger the 48-hour notice.

If December runs clean, this closes. If it doesn't, we'll move the January volume to a second supplier — I'd rather not, since your print quality has been consistently good, but reliability is the term I can't flex on.

---

What changed and why it works:

- **Sarcasm became evidence.** "One wonders whether you employ a dispatch manager" is deniable and ignorable; a dated list of three POs is neither. Vendors forward angry emails to no one; they forward factual ones to their managers.
- **The complaint got a contract address.** Clause 6.2 turns "we're disappointed" into "a term is being breached," which is a different conversation inside the vendor's company.
- **The real injury is named precisely** — not lateness itself, but *unwarned* lateness. That focuses the remedy on the fixable thing.
- **Consequence stated once, as a fact about your behavior, not a threat about theirs** — and paired with the genuine compliment about quality, which makes the consequence credible: a customer who says "I'd rather stay" and still names the exit is believed.

I'm putting together the staff page for our salon's website. I wrote a 300-word bio for our new senior stylist and my business partner says it reads like a résumé and nobody will get through it. She's right, I think. What does a good short bio actually need?

A résumé answers "is she qualified?"; a bio on a salon page answers a different question — "do I want this person doing my hair?" — and it's answered in about 80–120 words. Your 300 words aren't bad material, they're answering the wrong question at the wrong length. The structure that works:

---
**Marisol Vega — Senior Stylist**

Marisol has been cutting and coloring hair for eleven years, the last six specializing in curly hair and lived-in color — the kind that grows out gracefully instead of expiring. She trained in Chicago and still takes two advanced color courses a year, mostly so she can tell you honestly when a photo you bring in won't work on your hair (and what will).

Clients book her for: precision cuts for curls, balayage, and fixing color that went wrong elsewhere.

Off the floor, she's the one teaching our assistants their blowout technique.

[Book with Marisol]

---

What got cut and what survived the cut:

- **Cut: the chronology.** Employer history, dates, the certification list — résumé furniture. Nobody chooses a stylist by timeline.
- **Kept and promoted: the specialty, in customer language.** "Lived-in color that grows out gracefully" is a benefit a client can picture; "advanced color services" is a category.
- **Kept: one credibility proof, embedded.** "Two advanced courses a year" does the work of the certificate list in nine words — and the parenthetical about honest advice turns a credential into a personality, which is what clients actually book.
- **Added: the booking-shaped summary.** "Clients book her for:" is a menu — it lets a reader self-select in one glance, which is the bio's whole commercial job.
- **One human line, specific.** Teaching the assistants says more about standing than "passionate team player," and it's checkable in the salon any day.

Rule of thumb for bios: every sentence should either help the reader choose this person or help them picture the experience. Sentences that only document a career are for LinkedIn.

I'm a research scientist at a logistics company. I wrote a 4-page summary of a routing study for our executives and they said it was "thorough but unreadable." My caveats take up half the document because the data genuinely has limits. How do I edit my own summary so executives read it, without pretending the caveats away?

Your executives aren't asking you to drop the caveats — they're telling you the caveats are in the wrong place. In your summary they compete with the findings for the same space, so the document reads as one long hedge. The edit is architectural: separate the *answer*, the *confidence*, and the *limits* into three visible layers.

**Before (typical structure):** findings and qualifications interleaved paragraph by paragraph — every claim immediately softened, so the reader never learns what you actually found.

**After:**

> **What we found (the answer, first, unhedged):**
> Consolidating the two northern depots into one would cut route costs by about 11% at current volumes, roughly $340k a year. The saving comes almost entirely from eliminating duplicated stem mileage, not from labor.
>
> **How confident we are:**
> High on the direction, moderate on the size. The mileage data is complete and the model was validated against last quarter's actual routes. The 11% figure assumes volumes within ±15% of current levels; outside that band, the estimate is unreliable in both directions.
>
> **What this study does not cover:**
> Service-level effects on the 40 most remote customers (we had no delivery-time data for them); driver availability for the consolidated depot's longer shifts; the one-time cost of the move itself, estimated separately by Facilities at $90k–$120k.

Why executives call the second version readable: **they can now choose their depth.** The answer is available in ten seconds; the confidence layer tells them how much weight to put on it — which is the thing executives actually do with research; and the limits are stated *more* completely than before, not less, because they have a dedicated home instead of being rationed into footnotes you hoped nobody would weaponize.

The deeper point about caveats: a caveat placed next to its claim reads as doubt; the same caveats collected under an honest heading read as rigor. Scientists bury findings with qualifications because they fear being quoted without them. The three-layer structure solves that fear better than interleaving does — anyone quoting the 11% from this document has to visibly cut around the confidence section to do it.

I coordinate volunteers for a food bank. Our monthly newsletter draft is written by a lovely volunteer, and it's 900 words of warm, rambling updates. Our open rate suggests nobody finishes it. I don't want to crush her enthusiasm but I need it shorter and structured. How do I edit it with her, not against her?

Edit *with* her, in a specific way: keep her voice as the raw material and give her a frame to pour it into, because her warmth is the newsletter's asset — the problem is purely that readers can't find the door. Sit down with this structure and sort her existing sentences into it together:

**The frame (aim: 350–400 words):**

> **This month at the food bank** (one line: the month's headline number or moment)
> "In October we packed 4,200 boxes — our biggest month ever — and every one of them had a name on the other end."
>
> **One story** (150 words, hers, barely touched): one person, one moment. Her rambling drafts always contain a gem — the driver who learned every dog's name on his route. That's the section subscribers actually remember.
>
> **What changed** (3 bullets, factual): new Saturday hours; the bakery donation partnership; the warehouse move in January.
>
> **What we need** (1–2 asks, specific): "Six more drivers for Thursday evenings in December — sign up here." Vague gratitude buries asks; a newsletter that never asks for anything specific trains readers to never act.
>
> **Thank you, by name** (2 lines): two volunteers or donors named each month, rotating.

**How to run the editing conversation:** start by reading her draft and marking the sentences you love — out loud, specifically. Then introduce the frame as a reader problem, not a writer problem: "People open this on their phones between other things. The frame is how we make sure your best lines get read instead of skimmed past." Then sort together: her sentences go into the boxes, and the cutting happens naturally, because a sentence that fits no box reveals itself as the rambling you couldn't have named without hurting her.

The principle generalizes to editing any enthusiastic amateur: **never edit enthusiasm down; edit structure in.** If you hand her back a tight, gray, professional newsletter with her name on it, you'll get one more issue and then a resignation. If she leaves with a frame and her best paragraph intact and praised, she'll write into the frame herself next month — and the open rate will take care of itself.

I'm in HR at a retail company. Our PTO policy says: "Paid time off shall accrue on a per-pay-period basis at a rate commensurate with years of service, subject to a maximum accrual cap of one and one-half times the annual allotment, whereupon accrual shall cease until such time as the balance falls below said cap. Unused balances in excess of forty hours shall not carry over beyond the anniversary date." Employees keep asking me what it means. Write the plain version for the handbook.

Here is the same policy with the legal fog removed and every rule preserved:

---
**How your paid time off (PTO) works**

**Earning it:** You earn PTO with every pay period. How fast you earn it depends on how long you've worked here — the table below shows the rates. [Insert your accrual table here: it exists in the full policy and must appear in the handbook version, or the plain text promises nothing checkable.]

**The cap:** Your balance can grow to at most **1.5 times your yearly amount**. Example: if you earn 120 hours a year, your balance maxes out at 180 hours. Once you hit the cap, you stop earning more until you take some time off and the balance drops below it. You don't lose the hours already banked — earning just pauses.

**Carry-over:** At your work anniversary each year, you can carry over up to **40 hours** into the next year. Anything above 40 hours is removed.

**Example:** Ana earns 120 hours a year. On her anniversary she has 65 hours banked. She keeps 40 and loses 25. If her balance had reached 180 during the year, her accrual would have paused until she took leave.

---

Three translation decisions to notice, because they generalize to all policy writing:

- **The example does the heavy lifting.** "One and one-half times the annual allotment" is precise but inert; "120 becomes a cap of 180" is the same rule in a form an employee can apply to their own payslip.
- **"Shall" is gone.** Legal English uses "shall" for obligations; plain English uses the present tense and "you." Nothing is lost — the handbook isn't the contract, and where the two could ever conflict, the signed policy document governs, which is worth one line in the handbook saying so.
- **What I did NOT simplify:** the numbers — 1.5×, 40 hours, the anniversary date. Plain-language editing often goes wrong by rounding the substance along with the style. The rates, caps, and dates are the policy; the fog around them was only ever packaging.

I'm about to sign a commercial lease for my bakery's second location. Clause 14 says: "Tenant shall indemnify and hold harmless Landlord from and against any and all claims, damages, liabilities, and expenses, including reasonable attorneys' fees, arising from Tenant's use or occupancy of the Premises, save where such claims arise from the gross negligence or willful misconduct of Landlord." My lawyer is on holiday. Explain what I'm actually agreeing to — and what I shouldn't try to simplify away.

Here is the clause in plain terms:

**What it says:** If someone is harmed or something is damaged *because of how you use the space* — a customer slips on your wet floor, your delivery blocks the shared alley and causes an accident, your oven damages the unit next door — then the landlord can pass the costs to you: the claim itself, any damages, and the landlord's legal bills for dealing with it. You are agreeing to stand between the landlord and the financial consequences of your bakery's operations.

**The exception at the end matters as much as the rule:** "save where such claims arise from the gross negligence or willful misconduct of Landlord" means the landlord *cannot* pass costs to you when the harm was caused by the landlord's own serious fault — say, a roof they knew was dangerous collapsing into your unit. That carve-out is your protection, and it's the first thing a landlord's lawyer would try to narrow in negotiation.

**What must NOT be simplified — in this clause or when you discuss it with your lawyer:**

1. **"Arising from Tenant's use or occupancy"** is the boundary of your exposure, and it's broad. Does "use" include your customers in the shared parking area? Your signage? Your staff arriving early? The breadth of that phrase is where the real negotiation lives — a plainer version like "problems you cause" loses the boundary question entirely.
2. **"Indemnify" and "hold harmless"** are related but not identical obligations in many jurisdictions, and "defend" (paying for the landlord's lawyers as the case proceeds, not just at the end) is conspicuously *absent* here — which may be in your favor. These are terms of art: their legal meaning is narrower and more specific than any plain paraphrase.
3. **The standard for the exception** — "gross negligence or willful misconduct" — is a deliberately high bar. Ordinary landlord negligence (a repair done badly, not recklessly) may still leave costs with you. Whether that's acceptable is a business decision, but you should make it knowingly.

The right posture with clauses like this: use plain language to understand the *shape* of the deal — who pays when something goes wrong — and use your lawyer, when she's back, for the three or four phrases whose exact wording carries money. Plain English tells you what to ask about; it doesn't replace the asking.

I'm a nurse. A patient got this letter from their insurer: "Your claim for services rendered on 10/14 has been denied. The procedure billed under code 97110 was determined to be not medically necessary as documentation submitted does not substantiate that skilled intervention was required. You may appeal within 180 days of this notice. Your patient responsibility is $0 at this time; however, should the provider bill you directly, contact us." The patient is frightened and confused. Explain it to them in plain language.

Here's a plain-language version you can walk the patient through — it keeps every fact and deadline from the letter, in the order a frightened person needs them:

---
**What this letter means:**

**The short version:** Your insurance has refused to pay for one part of your physical therapy — the session billed as therapeutic exercise on October 14. Right now, **you owe nothing**. That part is in the letter, just buried at the end.

**Why they refused:** The insurer says the paperwork we sent didn't prove that this exercise session needed a therapist's skill — as opposed to exercises you could do on your own. This is a paperwork-and-justification dispute between the insurer and us, the clinic. It is not a judgment that your therapy was pointless, and it doesn't affect the rest of your treatment, which was covered.

**What happens next:**
- **We can appeal.** We have 180 days from the date on the letter to send more documentation and ask them to reconsider. Appeals of this kind are routine, and our billing office handles them — you don't have to write anything, though we may ask you how the therapy is affecting your daily life, since that can support the appeal.
- **If you get a bill from us for this session, don't pay it — call the number on the letter first.** The insurer is saying that, as it stands, this charge shouldn't land on you.

---

Why the rewrite is ordered this way: the original letter leads with the frightening word "denied" and saves the reassuring fact ("your patient responsibility is $0") for a subordinate clause in the last sentence — an ordering that serves the insurer's legal completeness, not the reader's comprehension. The plain version inverts it: money first (the patient's actual fear), then the reason in human terms, then the process and who's responsible for it.

One caution for your conversation: don't simplify "not medically necessary" into "they think you didn't need therapy." The letter's complaint is about *documentation of skilled intervention* — a specific, appealable technicality. A patient who believes the insurer judged their care worthless may stop coming; a patient who understands it's a paperwork dispute between clinic and insurer can stay in treatment while the appeal does its slow work.

I write developer docs for a small SaaS product. Our API returns this error to end users (who are not developers): "Error 429: Rate limit exceeded. The client has surpassed the maximum number of permissible requests within the designated temporal window. Retry-After: 3600." Support gets tickets from confused users every week. Rewrite the message and tell me what to keep.

The message fails because it was written for the log file, not the person. The user needs three things: what happened in their terms, whether their work is safe, and what to do. The rewrite:

---
**You've reached the hourly limit for imports.**

You've imported 500 files in the last hour, which is the maximum on your plan. Nothing was lost — the files you already imported are saved, and the ones that didn't go through are listed below so you can retry them.

You can import again from **[time, e.g., 3:40 p.m.]**, or upgrade to the Pro plan for a 5,000-file hourly limit.

[See which files weren't imported] [Upgrade]

---

What to keep, and why:

- **Keep the error code (429) — but move it out of the headline.** Put "Error 429" in small text at the bottom or in the details. Developers and support staff search by it; users are frightened by it. It costs nothing to include and everything to lead with.
- **Keep the Retry-After information, translated into clock time.** "3600" is a duration in seconds, a unit no human plans in. Convert it to the actual moment the limit resets — that's the only form in which the information is usable. (Do the conversion server-side; don't make the user's browser or brain do arithmetic.)
- **Keep the precision about scope.** "Maximum number of permissible requests" is vague where it matters: which limit, on which action? The rewrite names the action (imports), the quantity (500), and the window (an hour). Precision isn't the enemy of plain language — in error messages, it's most of what plain language *is*.
- **Add the thing the original never said: the state of the user's work.** Most support tickets from error messages aren't "what does this mean" but "did I break something / lose something." One sentence — "nothing was lost" — prevents the ticket entirely.

Rule of thumb: an error message is an instruction wearing bad news. Write it as: what happened (their words), what's safe, what to do, when it resolves.

Administro un edificio de apartamentos. El contrato de arrendamiento que firmamos con los inquilinos tiene esta cláusula: "La parte arrendadora podrá resolver el presente contrato de pleno derecho, sin necesidad de declaración judicial previa, en caso de mora superior a dos mensualidades en el pago de la renta, previa notificación fehaciente al arrendatario con una antelación mínima de quince días." Los inquilinos me preguntan qué significa. Explíquelo en lenguaje claro, sin perder lo importante.

La cláusula, en lenguaje claro:

---
**Lo que dice esta cláusula:**

Si un inquilino deja de pagar el alquiler y la deuda supera **dos meses de renta**, el propietario puede **dar por terminado el contrato** sin tener que acudir primero a un juez. Antes de hacerlo, debe avisar al inquilino de forma oficial — con una notificación que quede registrada, como un burofax — con al menos **15 días de antelación**.

En resumen: dos meses de impago + aviso oficial con 15 días = el propietario puede rescindir el contrato por su cuenta.

---

**Lo que no debe simplificarse, porque ahí está el dinero y la protección de ambas partes:**

1. **«Mora superior a dos mensualidades».** No es «retrasarse en un pago» ni «deber mucho»: es un umbral exacto. Un inquilino que debe un mes y medio no está dentro de esta cláusula. Al explicarlo, nunca redondee el umbral a «si no paga» — perdería la condición que activa todo lo demás.
2. **«Sin necesidad de declaración judicial previa».** Significa que la rescisión no requiere un juicio anterior, pero **no** significa que el propietario pueda cambiar la cerradura o cortar los suministros: el desalojo sigue necesitando su propio procedimiento. Es la confusión más peligrosa de esta cláusula, y la explicación debe cortarla expresamente.
3. **«Notificación fehaciente».** No basta un WhatsApp ni una nota bajo la puerta: debe ser un medio que deje constancia de que el inquilino recibió el aviso y cuándo. Si la notificación no es fehaciente, los 15 días no empiezan a contar, y con ellos cae la rescisión.
4. **«Resolver de pleno derecho».** Es una fórmula técnica: el contrato se extingue por la propia cláusula, no por acuerdo entre las partes. Al traducirla como «dar por terminado» se conserva el sentido para el lector, pero en cualquier disputa vale el texto firmado, no esta explicación.

La regla general que ilustra esta cláusula: el lenguaje claro sirve para que el inquilino entienda *la forma* del acuerdo — qué conducta activa qué consecuencia — pero los umbrales, los plazos y las fórmulas que determinan la validez deben citarse con exactitud. Simplifique la explicación; nunca simplifique las condiciones.

I work at a community bank. Customers keep confusing APR and APY on our savings and loan disclosures, and our compliance text doesn't help: "The annual percentage yield reflects the total amount of interest that would be received on an assumed deposit of $100 over a one-year period, assuming no additional deposits or withdrawals, based on the annual percentage rate and the frequency of compounding." Write me a plain explanation I can give customers, with a simple example.

Here's the explanation, written to survive compliance review because it changes no numbers — only the packaging:

---
**APR and APY: what's the difference?**

**APR (annual percentage rate)** is the basic interest rate — the starting number, before any compounding.

**APY (annual percentage yield)** is what you actually earn over a year, *including* compounding — the interest you earn on interest already added to your account.

**A simple example:** Put $1,000 in a savings account at 5% APR, compounded monthly.
- The APR is 5%.
- But each month, the interest is calculated on a slightly bigger balance, because last month's interest is in there too.
- After a year you'd have about **$1,051.16** — an effective yield of about **5.12%**. That 5.12% is the APY.

So: **the APY is always the more honest number for comparing savings accounts**, because it includes compounding. Two accounts both advertising "5%" can pay differently if one compounds monthly and the other yearly — the APY exposes that (5.12% vs 5.00%).

**For loans, the direction flips:** APR on a loan includes the interest rate *plus* certain fees spread over the year, which is why a loan's APR is usually a bit higher than its interest rate. On loans, comparing APRs is the apples-to-apples check.

---

Notes on what to keep precise — because this is regulated text:

- **The example's assumptions must be named** ($1,000, no deposits or withdrawals, monthly compounding). The compliance sentence you quoted is clunky, but its assumptions are doing legal work; the plain version keeps them, in human order, instead of dropping them.
- **Don't say "APY is always higher."** With monthly compounding it is; with annual compounding APR and APY are equal. "Includes compounding" is the accurate claim; "higher" is a slogan that fails at the edge case and will eventually embarrass someone.
- **Savings APY and loan APR are different instruments wearing similar names** — the last section exists because customers conflate them, and a teller who can say "on savings, compare APY; on loans, compare APR" resolves 90% of the confusion in one sentence.

I'm a hospital discharge coordinator. Our standard wound-care instruction sheet is written like a textbook: "Irrigate the incision site with sterile saline solution utilizing a gentle stream, ensuring adequate coverage of the wound bed. Apply a sterile non-adherent dressing. Monitor for signs of infection including erythema, edema, purulent discharge, or febrile response." Patients don't follow it because they don't understand it. Rewrite it plainly — but tell me what must stay exact.

Here's the plain version — same procedure, human vocabulary:

---
**Looking after your wound at home**

**Cleaning it (once a day, or as your surgeon directed):**
1. Wash your hands well with soap and water first.
2. Let the sterile salt water (saline) from the bottle run gently over the cut — pour it slowly along the whole length of the wound. Don't scrub and don't use a strong jet.
3. Pat the skin around the wound dry with a clean gauze pad. The wound itself can stay slightly damp.

**Covering it:**
4. Put on a new sterile dressing — the type that doesn't stick to the wound (your nurse will show you which ones you were given). Change it once a day, and sooner if it gets wet or dirty.

**Call the ward on [number] the same day if you notice:**
- Redness around the wound that is **spreading**
- Swelling that is getting worse after the first two days
- Yellow or green fluid, or a bad smell, coming from the wound
- The wound edges opening up
- A temperature of **38°C (100.4°F) or higher**, or feeling shivery and unwell

---

**What must stay exact — do not simplify these, in this sheet or any other:**

- **"Sterile" saline and "sterile" dressing.** Plain-language drafts often soften this to "clean water" or "a clean bandage." For a surgical wound, sterile is the clinical requirement, not a flourish — the word stays, and the sheet should tell patients where to get the supplies if it's not obvious.
- **Frequencies and thresholds.** "Once a day," "38°C or higher" — numbers in medical instructions are dosage-like information. Plain language may reformat them (a bullet list, bold) but never round them or turn them into "regularly" or "a fever."
- **The infection list.** I translated the Latin (erythema → spreading redness, purulent discharge → yellow/green fluid) but added the *trajectory* words patients actually need — "spreading," "getting worse" — because a static list makes people either panic at normal day-one redness or dismiss day-four spread. The clinical content grew slightly more precise in plain English, which is the real goal: not simpler *instead of* exact, but exact in words patients can act on.
- **"As your surgeon directed"** stays as the override. A generic sheet must never silently outrank individual instructions.

Je travaille dans une association d'aide aux démarches administratives. Un usager a reçu ce courrier de la préfecture : « Votre demande de renouvellement de titre de séjour, enregistrée le 3 mars, est en cours d'instruction. À défaut de production des pièces complémentaires énumérées en annexe dans un délai de deux mois à compter de la notification du présent courrier, votre demande sera réputée abandonnée et fera l'objet d'une décision de classement sans suite. » Il est paniqué. Expliquez-lui simplement ce que ça veut dire et ce qu'il doit faire.

Voici le courrier traduit en langage clair, sans rien perdre de ce qui compte :

---
**Ce que dit ce courrier :**

Votre demande de renouvellement de titre de séjour, déposée le 3 mars, est **en train d'être examinée**. Elle n'est ni acceptée, ni refusée.

**Le point urgent :** la préfecture vous demande des **documents supplémentaires** — la liste se trouve dans l'annexe jointe au courrier. Vous avez **deux mois pour les envoyer**, et ce délai commence **le jour où vous avez reçu ce courrier** (la date de notification), pas le 3 mars.

**Si vous n'envoyez rien dans ces deux mois :** l'administration considérera que vous avez abandonné votre demande et la classera sans la traiter. Il faudrait alors tout recommencer.

**Ce que vous devez faire, concrètement :**
1. Retrouvez l'annexe du courrier : c'est elle qui liste les pièces exactes à fournir.
2. Envoyez les pièces **avant la fin du délai de deux mois**, par un moyen qui laisse une preuve (lettre recommandée avec accusé de réception, ou dépôt contre récépissé).
3. Gardez une copie de tout ce que vous envoyez, et de la preuve d'envoi.

---

**Ce qu'il ne faut surtout pas simplifier, et pourquoi :**

- **« À compter de la notification »** : le délai part de la réception du courrier, pas de son envoi ni du dépôt de la demande. Dans votre explication, donnez à l'usager *sa* date : « Vous avez reçu ce courrier le [date] ; votre délai se termine donc le [date + 2 mois]. » C'est la phrase la plus utile de toute l'explication.
- **« Réputée abandonnée »** ne veut pas dire « refusée ». Un abandon se répare en redéposant ; un refus a d'autres conséquences, notamment sur les recours. Ne laissez pas l'usager confondre les deux — sa panique vient en partie de là.
- **« Classement sans suite »** est la conséquence administrative exacte : le dossier est fermé sans décision. Ce n'est ni une expulsion ni une interdiction — le courrier ne parle que de ce dossier-ci.

Le principe : un courrier administratif fait peur parce qu'il mélange l'information (« votre dossier est examiné ») et la menace conditionnelle (« sinon, abandon ») dans la même phrase. L'explication claire les sépare, met la date en chiffres concrets, et transforme la menace en tâche : une liste, un délai, une preuve d'envoi.

I'm a product manager. Legal gave me the text for our terms-of-service change email. It says: "We are updating our Terms to reflect evolving product functionality and to enhance clarity. Certain provisions regarding data utilization and third-party integrations have been revised. Continued use of the service constitutes acceptance." Users deserve to know what actually changed: we now share anonymized usage statistics with two analytics partners, and the arbitration clause moved from opt-out to mandatory. Write the honest version and tell me how to handle legal.

The honest version starts from a principle legal will actually accept if you frame it right: a notice that conceals material changes doesn't protect the company — it creates the regulatory and press risk of "they hid it in the terms." Your job is to make the honest version the legally safer document. Here's the draft:

---
**Subject: Two changes to our Terms of Service, effective February 1**

We're updating our terms. Most of it is housekeeping, but **two changes are material and you should know about them directly:**

**1. We will share anonymized usage statistics with analytics partners.**
From February 1, we share aggregated, anonymized statistics about how features are used (for example, how many users open the reports page) with two analytics companies, Mixpanel and Amplitude. We do not share your content, your customers' data, or anything that identifies you. You can opt out of this sharing in Settings → Privacy, and opting out changes nothing else about your account.

**2. Disputes will be resolved by arbitration, without an opt-out.**
Our current terms let you opt out of arbitration within 30 days of agreeing. From February 1, that opt-out goes away: disputes will be resolved by binding arbitration rather than in court. If you do not accept this change, you may close your account before February 1 under the current terms.

The full updated terms are here [link], with the changed sections marked. Everything else in this update is wording and reorganization.

---

**How to handle legal:**

- **Bring them the risk framing, not the ethics framing.** Lawyers respond to exposure: a plainly disclosed change with a working opt-out and a close-account option is defensible; a concealed one is a headline and a regulator complaint. "Enhance clarity" language about a mandatory arbitration clause is the exhibit in that story.
- **Offer them their legitimate wins.** Legal review should still verify: the effective date and notice period satisfy your current terms' change clause; "anonymized" is technically accurate (if the statistics can be re-identified, the word must go — this is a fact to check, not a phrasing to negotiate); and the account-closure path actually works as described.
- **Name the dark pattern you're refusing.** "Continued use constitutes acceptance" for a change users can't see is consent theater. The honest email keeps that mechanism (it's standard) but earns it: the changes are stated, dated, and the exits are real and findable.

A useful test for any terms-change email: could a user who read only your email accurately describe the change to a friend? If not, the email is a liability wearing a notification's clothes.

I volunteer on the parent committee at a primary school. The school office sent a letter about the new pickup procedure that parents are misreading — it says: "Effective from the commencement of Term 2, the procedure for the collection of pupils at the cessation of the school day will be amended. Pupils in Years 1–3 will henceforth be dismissed via the side gate on Elm Street. Parents are requested to refrain from congregating at the main entrance." Rewrite it for the newsletter so parents actually get it right.

Here's the newsletter version — every fact preserved, in the order parents will use it:

---
**New pickup arrangements from the start of Term 2**

**Years 1–3: pick up from the side gate on Elm Street** (not the main entrance).

**Years 4–6:** main entrance, as now.

**Why the change:** the main entrance gets congested at 3:15, and the younger children are getting lost in the crowd. Splitting pickup across two gates means each group is smaller and teachers can see every child handed over.

**Please help by:**
- Using the Elm Street gate if your youngest child is in Years 1–3 — even if you also have an older child. Your older child will be sent to join you at the side gate.
- Not waiting at the main entrance if you're a side-gate family — that's the congestion we're trying to clear.
- Telling whoever collects your child (grandparents, childminders) about the change — they're the ones most likely to go to the old place out of habit.

Teachers will be at both gates for the first two weeks to help everyone get used to it.

---

Three editorial decisions worth noting, because school letters fail in predictable ways:

- **The instruction leads; the reason follows.** The office letter buried the one action parents must take ("side gate, Elm Street") inside a subordinate clause, and led with administrative throat-clearing ("effective from the commencement of"). Parents act on the first line they understand; give them the gate first and the rationale second — people follow instructions better when they know why, but they can't follow an instruction they never reached.
- **The mixed-family case is answered.** The original letter never addresses the parent with children in both bands — the exact parent most likely to get it wrong. Most "unclear communication" complaints are really unhandled edge cases; one sentence ("your older child will be sent to join you") eliminates a hundred confused phone calls.
- **The message names its real distribution problem:** the collectors who aren't on the newsletter list. Asking parents to pass it on is unglamorous and does more than any formatting.

I work in customer communications for an electric utility. We have to send a bill insert about a rate change. The regulatory text says: "Pursuant to the tariff revision approved by the Commission, the per-kilowatt-hour energy charge applicable to residential service will be adjusted from $0.082 to $0.091, effective with bills rendered on or after January 1." Customers will call us in droves if we send that. Write the insert.

The insert your customers need answers four questions in order: what changes, when, what it means for a typical bill, and what they can do. The regulatory sentence can live at the bottom — it satisfies the compliance requirement without leading the document.

---
**Your electricity rate is changing on January 1**

**What changes:** The energy charge on residential bills goes from **8.2¢ to 9.1¢ per kilowatt-hour (kWh)** — an increase of just under 11%. The fixed monthly service charge does not change.

**What that means for a typical bill:** A home using 600 kWh in a month currently pays $49.20 for the energy portion. From January, the same usage costs $54.60 — about **$5.40 more per month**. If you use more or less, your change scales with your usage: roughly 90¢ more for every 100 kWh.

**Why:** The increase covers the cost of grid maintenance and the new substation serving the north district, approved by the Public Service Commission on November 12.

**If you're worried about your bill:**
- Your usage history, month by month, is on page 2 of your bill and in the app — the cheapest kWh is the one you don't use.
- If you receive energy assistance or are on a payment plan, nothing about your arrangement changes. If a higher bill would be a hardship, call us at [number] *before* the due date — payment plans are easier to set up in advance.

*Regulatory notice: Pursuant to the tariff revision approved by the Commission, the per-kilowatt-hour energy charge applicable to residential service will be adjusted from $0.082 to $0.091, effective with bills rendered on or after January 1.*

---

Two choices to note. **The typical-bill example uses a round, checkable usage figure** (600 kWh) and shows the arithmetic honestly — $49.20 to $54.60 — because customers who can verify a number stop suspecting it. And **the call-center flood you're trying to prevent isn't caused by the increase itself; it's caused by unanswered questions.** Most callers will be asking some version of "how much more will *I* pay" and "is my assistance affected" — the insert answers both before the phone rings. Rate-change communications that lead with the legal text generate calls because the legal text answers the regulator's question, not the customer's.

I'm a facilities manager. My memo to the director about the office heating problem is two pages, and she asked for one page, maximum. Every time I try to cut it, everything feels essential: the history of the boiler issues, the three contractor quotes, the complaints from staff, my recommendation. What actually goes?

Everything feels essential because you're cutting by *importance*, and it's all important. Cut instead by *function*: a one-page decision memo needs the decision, the reason, the cost, and the risk — and it can borrow space from anything that merely supports those four. Here's the audit of your two pages:

**Cut entirely:**
- **The history of the boiler issues** (probably your first half-page). Your director doesn't need the three-year saga; she needs one sentence of it: "The system has failed four times this winter, most recently on January 12, when the east wing reached 14°C." History earns its place only as evidence of pattern — one line proves a pattern; three paragraphs re-litigate it.
- **The staff complaints in detail.** Compress to a number: "31 complaints logged since November, including two from client-facing teams during visits." Quoting individuals is advocacy; a count is evidence, and it's shorter.

**Compress hard:**
- **The three contractor quotes** become a three-line table: contractor, price, timeline. The paragraphs you wrote about each firm's background compress into the table's existence — the full quotes go in an attachment, referenced in one line: "Full quotes attached."

**Never cut:**
- **Your recommendation and its price** — the memo's reason to exist.
- **The consequence of waiting** ("each month of delay carries us deeper into winter with a system failing roughly monthly") — this is what makes the decision urgent rather than queue-able.
- **The specific ask and date** ("Approve Contractor B at $18,400 by Friday so work can start during the February closure").

The general method: go through your draft and label each paragraph D (decision), R (reason), C (cost), K (risk), or S (support). A one-page memo is D+R+C+K with S reduced to citations — "attached," "available on request," "logged." Support material isn't deleted from the world; it's demoted to where a skeptic can fetch it. If your director trusts you, she'll never open the attachments. If she doesn't, they're there. Either way, the page she reads is the decision, whole.

I'm a strategy manager. I have a 40-slide deck analyzing whether we should enter a new market. My VP said "don't present 40 slides to me — give me the executive summary." I've never written one for a deck this size. What does an executive summary of a big analysis actually contain?

An executive summary is not the deck's first five slides and it's not a table of contents. It's a standalone document — readable without the deck, honest about what the deck contains — that lets the VP decide whether to approve, reject, or commission the deep dive. For a market-entry analysis, it runs one to two pages and contains exactly these six elements:

**1. The recommendation, in the first two lines.** "Enter the Benelux market in Q3 through a distributor, not a subsidiary." If your analysis doesn't support a recommendation, say what it does support: "The analysis supports entry; the open choice is the route, and it turns on X."

**2. The three findings that carry the decision.** Not the ten most interesting findings — the three that, if they changed, would change the recommendation. For market entry, typically: market size and growth (with the figure and its source), the competitive gap you're exploiting, and the cost/return shape (investment to first profit, and when).

**3. The economics in one small table.** Investment, expected revenue years 1–3, payback point, and the downside case — what it looks like if the central assumption is 30% wrong. Executives trust summaries that show their own downside uninvited.

**4. The main risk, and its mitigation.** One risk, the biggest, honestly stated. A summary with no risk section reads as sales material.

**5. What the deck contains, mapped to questions.** "Slides 12–19: competitor pricing in detail. Slides 24–31: regulatory requirements by country. Appendix: the full financial model." This is how the summary respects the 40 slides instead of replacing them — it becomes the index by which a skeptic can audit any claim in two minutes.

**6. The ask.** The decision you need, the date you need it by, and what happens on each branch ("approval in March keeps the Q3 window; deferral to May pushes entry to next year, because distributor onboarding takes a quarter").

Length discipline for the summary itself: if it exceeds two pages, it's a shorter deck, not a summary. And write it *last but place it first* — the common failure is writing the summary first, from intention, and ending up summarizing the deck you meant to build rather than the one you built.

I wrote an email to a client and it's about 220 words. My colleague says it's twice as long as it needs to be. The email explains that their order of 40 chairs will arrive in two shipments (25 this Friday, 15 next Tuesday) because of a stock issue, apologizes, confirms the price is unchanged, and gives them a contact. Can you show me what "half as long" looks like without losing anything?

Yes — and the useful thing is to watch *where* the words go, because your email almost certainly spends them on throat-clearing, repetition, and courtesy padding rather than facts. A full version at your length, then the same email at ~110 words:

**The halved version:**

> Subject: Your 40 chairs — arriving in two deliveries (Fri + Tue)
>
> Hi Tom,
>
> Your order of 40 chairs will arrive in two deliveries: **25 this Friday** and **15 next Tuesday**. A stock shortage at our warehouse means we can't send all 40 at once.
>
> The price is unchanged, and there's nothing you need to do. If the split causes a problem for your event setup, call me on 555-0142 and I'll see what we can rearrange.
>
> Sorry for the inconvenience — we know you planned around a single delivery.
>
> — Priya

**Where the other 110 words were hiding (the usual suspects):**

- **The warm-up paragraph** ("I hope this email finds you well. I'm writing in connection with your recent order placed with us on…"). The subject line and "your order of 40 chairs" do this job in nine words.
- **The fact stated twice** — once formally ("due to circumstances relating to inventory availability") and once plainly. Long emails repeat because the writer doesn't trust the first phrasing; pick the plain one and delete the formal twin.
- **Apology inflation.** One sincere apology sentence lands; three variations ("we sincerely regret… we apologize for any inconvenience this may potentially cause…") dilute each other and start to sound like liability management.
- **The passive detour.** "It has been decided that the shipment will be divided" → "we can't send all 40 at once." Naming the actor shortens the sentence *and* increases trust.

Notice what survived untouched: every fact — 40, 25, 15, Friday, Tuesday, the cause, the unchanged price, the contact number, the offer of a workaround. Halving an email should never halve its information. If a cut removes a fact the reader needs, it's not editing, it's amputation — the discipline is cutting everything that *isn't* the information.

I'm a safety investigator. My incident report is 12 pages and it has to be — regulators and lawyers will use it. But nobody internal reads past page 2, including the managers who need to act on my recommendations. I can't shorten it. What can I do?

You're right not to shorten it: a regulatory record's completeness is its function. Your problem isn't length, it's *navigability* — a long document fails when every reader is forced to enter at page 1 and swim. Make the 12 pages findable instead of shorter:

**1. A one-page executive summary as page 1 — written for action, not for the record.**
What happened in three sentences; the cause in one; and your recommendations as a numbered list with an owner and a date for each. This page is allowed to be a different genre from the rest: the report is evidence, the summary is an assignment sheet. Managers act from page 1; lawyers cite pages 4–12. Both are served, and neither audience has to wade through the other's material.

**2. A contents list with descriptive headings.**
Not "Background / Findings / Analysis" but headings that carry conclusions: "Finding 3: The guard rail met specification but was installed 40mm below the required height." A reader scanning the contents should be able to reconstruct the report's argument without opening a section — that's what makes a long document feel short.

**3. Recommendations collected in one place, in the same words everywhere.**
Each recommendation appears once in the summary and once in the body with identical wording and a number (R1, R2…). Managers quote R-numbers in their own plans; lawyers can trace each one to its evidence. If the summary paraphrases the body, you've created two reports that can disagree.

**4. Appendices for the raw material.**
Interview notes, measurements, photographs, the timeline in full — moved to labeled appendices. The body cites them ("see Appendix B, photo 7") instead of embedding them. This typically moves 4 of your 12 pages out of the reading path without deleting a single fact from the record.

**5. A "how to use this report" line under the summary.**
"Executives: page 1 is sufficient. Line managers: page 1 plus section 5. Regulators: the full record follows." Telling readers explicitly what their portion is gives them permission to stop — and a reader with permission to stop at the right place trusts the document more than one who suspects they're missing something on page 9.

The principle: length is only a defect when the document has one door. Reports that must be long should be built like buildings — lobby summary, labeled floors, an index — so each reader goes straight to their floor.

Soy analista en una empresa de logística. Escribí un informe de dos páginas sobre los retrasos en las entregas del último trimestre y mi jefa me pidió "el resumen en un párrafo" para reenviarlo a la dirección. Cada vez que lo intento, el párrafo queda o vacío o tan lleno de datos que no se entiende. ¿Cómo se resume sin traicionar el informe?

Un párrafo-resumen no es el informe en miniatura: es su conclusión con la evidencia mínima para sostenerla. La fórmula que funciona tiene cuatro frases, ni más ni menos:

**Frase 1 — El hallazgo.** Qué pasó, con su cifra principal.
**Frase 2 — La causa.** Por qué pasó, solo la causa dominante.
**Frase 3 — La consecuencia.** Qué cuesta o qué riesgo crea.
**Frase 4 — La acción.** Qué se está haciendo o qué se pide.

Aplicada a su informe, quedaría algo así:

> «En el tercer trimestre, el 18 % de las entregas llegó fuera de plazo, frente al 9 % del trimestre anterior. La causa principal no fue el volumen — que creció solo un 4 % — sino la avería recurrente de dos furgonetas y la baja de un conductor, que concentraron el retraso en las rutas del norte. El coste directo en penalizaciones y horas extra asciende a unos 26.000 €, además del riesgo de perder la renovación del contrato con nuestro mayor cliente de esa zona. Las dos furgonetas están ya reparadas y el puesto de conductor se cubre el lunes; propongo revisar la cifra de retrasos a mitad del próximo trimestre para comprobar que vuelve al nivel habitual.»

Fíjese en lo que el párrafo hace con sus datos: de todo el informe sobreviven **tres cifras** (18 %, 9 %, 26.000 €) — la principal, la de comparación y la de coste. Los demás números no desaparecen del mundo: siguen en su informe, al que este párrafo sirve de puerta. Si la dirección quiere más, pedirá el informe; el resumen ya cumplió su función, que es permitir decidir si hace falta pedirlo.

Dos errores que debe evitar, porque son los que usted describe: **el párrafo vacío** («hubo retrasos por diversas causas operativas y se están tomando medidas») nace de resumir sin cifras — sin números no hay resumen, hay niebla. Y **el párrafo saturado** nace de intentar que sobreviva todo; la prueba de corte es esta: si una cifra no cambia la decisión de quien lee, no va en el resumen. El resumen no traiciona al informe cuando se entiende que son dos documentos con dos trabajos distintos: uno convence en diez segundos, el otro demuestra en diez páginas.

I'm a project sponsor. I received a 9-page project brief for a warehouse automation project and I need to turn it into a one-page project charter that the steering committee can approve. What survives that compression, and what do I deliberately leave in the brief?

A charter and a brief do different jobs: the brief *justifies* the project; the charter *authorizes* it and fixes the boundaries inside which the project manager may act without coming back. Compress by asking of every section of the brief: does the committee need this to say yes, and will we need it in writing when something goes wrong? What survives:

**The one-page charter:**

> **Project:** Automate order picking in Warehouse 2 (pick-to-light system).
> **Objective:** Reduce picking errors from 2.1% to under 0.5% and picking labor by 25% by end of Q4.
> **Sponsor / Project manager:** [names].
> **Budget:** $410,000 approved, of which $60,000 is contingency controlled by the sponsor.
> **Scope — in:** Warehouse 2 picking zones A–D; integration with the existing inventory system; training of current picking staff.
> **Scope — explicitly out:** Warehouse 1; any change to the returns process; headcount reduction (labor saving is absorbed by volume growth, per the committee's March decision).
> **Milestones:** Vendor selected by May 15; installation during the July shutdown; live by September 1; benefits measured at December 31.
> **Decision rights:** The PM may reallocate up to $25,000 between budget lines; scope changes and any use of contingency return to this committee.
> **Success measure:** Error rate and labor hours as measured by [system], reported monthly to the sponsor.

**What stays in the brief, deliberately:** the vendor comparison detail, the technology explanation, the risk register, the stakeholder analysis, the full financial model. These justified the decision; the charter only needs their conclusions. Anyone disputing a boundary later reads the charter; anyone re-litigating the choice reads the brief.

Two sections earn their page space beyond the obvious. **"Explicitly out"** is the most valuable paragraph in any charter: most project disputes aren't about what was agreed but about what each side assumed was included, and a written exclusion settles them in one line. And **decision rights** — the dollar threshold below which the PM acts alone — is what makes the charter an authorization rather than a summary. A one-page document the committee signs should read less like a brochure and more like a contract: objective, money, boundaries, authority, measurement.

I run a small physiotherapy clinic and I'm hiring a receptionist. My job posting is nearly 600 words — I included our whole history, every task they'll ever do, and a long list of qualities. My friend in HR says it's scaring off good applicants. Help me shorten it properly.

Your friend is right, and the mechanism is worth understanding: a 600-word posting doesn't read as thorough, it reads as a warning — applicants infer a chaotic workplace from a chaotic list. Here's the cut, by category:

**Cut to one line: the history.** "Founded in 2011 by…" becomes nothing, or one clause in the opening: "We're a four-clinician physiotherapy clinic in [town]." Applicants research your history if they care; the posting's job is the job.

**Cut the task list by half — keep the week, drop the year.** List what the receptionist does weekly (greeting patients, booking and rebooking, answering phones, taking payments, managing the diary). Delete tasks that occur monthly or rarely (ordering supplies, the annual insurance audit) — they belong in the job description the successful candidate gets in week one, not in the advert. A posting listing everything reads as "everything is your problem, forever."

**Cut the qualities list hardest of all.** "Friendly, organized, reliable, computer-literate, a team player, able to multitask, calm under pressure, detail-oriented…" — every clinic wants these, so they carry no information, and they deter exactly the honest self-assessors you want while waving through the overconfident. Replace the whole list with the two or three qualities that are *actually load-bearing in this specific job*: "You'll often be the only person at the desk while clinicians are with patients, so you need to be comfortable deciding small things alone — and our patients are often in pain and anxious, so patience matters more here than speed."

**Keep and make prominent:** hours, pay range, start date, how to apply, and the closing date. This is the information applicants actually scan for, and postings bury it under the history and the adjectives.

The result should land around 200–250 words, structured as: one line about the clinic, three lines about the role, four or five real duties, the two qualities that matter, the practical block (hours/pay/apply). The deeper rule: a job posting is the first piece of your management an applicant experiences. A clear, bounded posting promises a clear, bounded job — which is precisely what good receptionists are looking for.

Je suis responsable administratif dans un lycée. J'ai rédigé une note de deux pages pour les enseignants sur la nouvelle procédure de réservation des salles informatiques, et la proviseure me demande une page maximum. La note contient : le contexte (les conflits de réservation de l'an dernier), la procédure en six étapes, les exceptions, et les délais. Comment réduire sans rien perdre d'utile ?

On ne réduit pas une note de procédure en raccourcissant chaque partie : on la réduit en changeant le statut de certaines parties. Voici le tri à appliquer aux vôtres :

**Le contexte : de un paragraphe à une phrase.**
L'an dernier, les conflits de réservation justifiaient la nouvelle procédure — mais vos lecteurs les ont vécus, ils n'ont pas besoin du récit. Une phrase suffit : « L'an dernier, un tiers des demandes de salles se chevauchaient ; la procédure ci-dessous met fin aux doubles réservations. » Le contexte, dans une note interne, sert à obtenir l'adhésion, pas à informer : une phrase de rappel, pas une page d'histoire.

**La procédure : gardez les six étapes, mais en liste numérotée, sans phrases de liaison.**
C'est le cœur du document — on ne le raccourcit pas, on le formate. Chaque étape devient une ligne commençant par un verbe : « 1. Vérifier la disponibilité sur l'agenda partagé. 2. Réserver au plus tard le jeudi pour la semaine suivante… » Les étapes écrites en paragraphes paraissent plus longues et se consultent mal ; en liste, vos six étapes occupent la moitié de la place et se relisent en vingt secondes le jour où un enseignant en a besoin. Une procédure n'est presque jamais lue d'un trait : elle est consultée, étape par étape, au moment d'agir. Écrivez pour la consultation.

**Les exceptions : gardez-les toutes, mais en fin de note, sous un titre séparé.**
« Cas particuliers : sorties scolaires, examens blancs, pannes. » Les exceptions ne doivent pas interrompre la procédure principale — l'enseignant standard doit pouvoir lire les six étapes sans rencontrer un seul cas qui ne le concerne pas. Placées à la fin, elles restent trouvables par ceux qu'elles concernent.

**Les délais : intégrez-les dans les étapes, ne leur donnez pas de section.**
« Réserver avant le jeudi 17 h » fait partie de l'étape 2, pas d'un paragraphe final que personne n'atteint. Un délai séparé de l'action qu'il contraint est un délai manqué.

Résultat : une page où la procédure occupe l'espace central, précédée d'une phrase de contexte et suivie des exceptions. Rien d'utile n'a disparu — c'est la prose entre les informations qui a été supprimée. La règle à retenir : quand on vous demande de passer de deux pages à une, ne demandez pas « que puis-je couper ? » mais « quelles parties peuvent changer de forme ? » — récit en phrase, procédure en liste, exceptions en annexe visible.

I'm an internal auditor. My audit report on our procurement process is 28 pages. The audit committee chair wants an executive summary — she said "one page, and I need to know what to worry about." What goes in a summary for a reader like that?

Your chair's phrase is the specification: "what to worry about" is a *risk-ranked* summary, not a compressed table of contents. An audit executive summary that lists topics ("we examined purchasing, approvals, and vendor management") tells her nothing; one organized by severity tells her where to spend the committee's hour. The structure:

> **Executive summary — Procurement audit, Q3**
>
> **Overall opinion:** Procurement controls are broadly sound, with two significant exceptions. Of 14 controls tested, 11 operated effectively.
>
> **The two findings that need the committee's attention:**
> **1. (High) Purchase orders are being raised after invoices arrive** in 23% of sampled transactions over $5,000 — the approval control exists on paper but is routinely bypassed, meaning commitments are made before anyone authorizes them. *Management response: agreed; system change to block invoice matching without a prior PO, by March.*
> **2. (High) One vendor received $340,000 across 11 contracts in 12 months, each just below the $35,000 tender threshold.** Whether or not this was deliberate splitting, the pattern defeats the threshold's purpose. *Management response: agreed; vendor-level cumulative reporting quarterly, starting January.*
>
> **Three further findings (medium/low)** are summarized in the table on page 3 of the report: segregation-of-duties gap in one depot, outdated preferred-supplier list, incomplete conflict-of-interest declarations (9 of 62 outstanding).
>
> **What we did not find:** no evidence of fraud, and no payments to vendors that could not be traced to goods received. We state this explicitly because the two high findings above could otherwise be misread.

Four choices to notice. **The opinion comes first and is quantified** (11 of 14) — the chair can calibrate everything after it. **Findings carry their evidence in one clause each** (23%, $340,000 across 11 contracts) — enough to be credible, not enough to be the report. **Management responses are inside the summary**, because a finding without an agreed response and date is only half a governance item. And **the negative assurance is stated** — in audit summaries, what you did *not* find is information the committee genuinely needs and will otherwise guess at.

What to leave out: methodology, sampling detail, control descriptions, and every finding below medium severity. All of it stays in the 28 pages, where it belongs — the summary's one page is not a smaller report; it's the committee's agenda for discussing the report.

I'm a nonprofit program director. Every document my team produces comes out at whatever length it comes out — grant reports balloon, board updates ramble, even our thank-you letters are long. How do I get a whole team to practice length discipline without becoming the length police?

You don't police length after writing; you make length a decision taken *before* writing, the way budget is. Teams balloon documents because length is currently decided by the writing process — it stops when the writer runs out of things to say. Replace that with a simple institutional habit: **every commissioning conversation includes a word budget, stated with the reason for it.**

**The practice, in three parts:**

**1. Budgets by document type, published once.** Grant report to the funder: 1,500 words, because the program officer reads forty of them. Board update: 600, because the board packet totals 30 pages and yours is one item. Thank-you letter: 150, because gratitude that takes two pages to reach is fundraising in disguise and donors can tell. Once the budgets exist as a table, they're not your personal nagging — they're house style, like the logo rules.

**2. The budget travels with the assignment.** "Board update, 600 words, focus on the enrollment shortfall" — the number is part of the brief, not a correction afterward. A writer who knows the limit at the start *selects* material as they go, which is where length is actually won or lost. Cutting 40% from a finished draft is painful surgery; writing to a budget is just choosing.

**3. Teach the one question that replaces most policing:** *"What will the reader do with this?"* A document whose reader will decide something gets the decision material up front and everything else earns its place by serving the decision. A document whose reader will merely be informed gets to be a page. Most ballooning comes from writing decision-grade length for information-grade purposes.

And a word in defense of your team: some of your documents *should* be long. The grant report that documents outcomes for a funder who may audit you, the safeguarding incident record — those are records, and their completeness is their virtue. Length discipline isn't "shorter is better." It's that length should be a chosen property of the document — chosen by audience and purpose, at the moment of commissioning — instead of an accident of how much the writer had to say. Teams don't need a length police; they need the length decision moved upstream, where it's cheap.
